GeoGPT · Guided geology investigation

Has the sand ended—or has the image blurred it?

Could a sand bed continue between boreholes where seismic reflections merge?

The geological task

When tracing a possible aquifer or reservoir between boreholes, a geologist may see a reflection fade or merge. That can reflect rock geometry, but it can also reflect the seismic pulse. We start with a known hypothetical sand wedge and ask GeoGPT to calculate its image. Knowing the rocks lets us isolate an imaging effect before making a field interpretation.

Your role: inspect the evidence and explain a bounded conclusion. GeoGPT performs the requested analysis. All required settings are already supplied.

Four useful words

Reflection
A returning seismic signal from a contrast between rocks.

Trace
One vertical column of the calculated seismic image.

Two-way time
Travel time down to an interface and back.

Frequency
Cycles per second; here higher frequency makes a shorter pulse.

The idea in plain language

A seismic pulse travels down through the ground. At a contrast in rock properties, some energy returns to the receiver. In this model, reflections return from the top and bottom of a sand bed. A thick bed separates the arrivals in time. In a thin bed, the returning pulses overlap and add together, changing their apparent shape and brightness. Higher frequency gives a shorter pulse here. We calculate the image from known rocks, then change only the pulse. This is forward modelling; we are not solving for unknown rocks.

Minutes 5–15

Compute a checked image

Do this

Send Prompt 1. When the reply finishes, open wedge-30Hz.png under Research Space. Read the short check table, then inspect the two panels using the guide below.

Why: The yellow bed is the input geology; the colored lower panel is its calculated reflection signal. Its vertical axis is time, not depth. Red and blue are positive and negative signal amplitude, not different rock types. Dashed lines mark the supplied top and base times; signal peaks need not coincide with them. At the very left edge the bed thickness is zero. The prompt supplies every model setting and runs two simple physical checks.

Work in English for a general geology graduate student. This is a fully specified teaching task. Execute the task rather than asking for intended use, validation purpose, thresholds, hypotheses, software, approval or other preferences. Ask only if a named input is missing or unreadable; name it and stop. Do not fabricate execution, observations or citations. Use short plain-language final answers, not JSON or a code dump. End with “Finished. Return to the handout.” Do not append a question or an offer. Question: could a sand bed continue between boreholes even where its top and base cannot be separated in a seismic image? Build and execute the following hypothetical wedge; this is not a real field survey. Use independent vertical normal-incidence traces, two primary reflections only. Shale above and below: velocity 2000 m/s, density 2000 kg/m3. Sand: 2500 m/s, 2200 kg/m3. x=0..1000 m every 25 m; sand thickness h=0.08*x; top depth 400 m. Top two-way time .400 s; base .400+2*h/2500 s. Time 0.300 to 0.550 s every .0005 s, inclusive. Rtop=(rho_sand*v_sand-rho_shale*v_shale)/(rho_sand*v_sand+rho_shale*v_shale); Rbase=-Rtop. w(u)=(1-2*(pi*f*u)^2)*exp(-(pi*f*u)^2). s(t,x)=Rtop*w(t-top)+Rbase*w(t-base), using analytical time shifts. No independent trace normalization, noise, multiples, attenuation or lateral wave propagation. Use f=30 Hz. Save wedge-model.py, wedge-values.csv (distance_m,thickness_m,time_ms,amplitude), and wedge-30Hz.png. Figure: 14x12 inch canvas with explicit separate axes rectangles, geology [0.12,0.65,0.72,0.27], seismic [0.12,0.24,0.72,0.29], colorbar [0.87,0.24,0.025,0.29]. Do not use tight_layout or constrained_layout. Geology: depth350..520 m downward, sand yellow/shale grey. Seismic:300..550 ms downward, signed amplitude blue-white-red fixed -0.25..+0.25; distance0..1000m. Overlay thin dashed true top/base times. Short titles and readable labels, caption below y=.08. Before interpreting: execute equal-impedance and zero-thickness tests, tolerance1e-10; fix failures and restore baseline. Read the baseline CSV to report amplitude at x=0 and location of strongest absolute amplitude; do not confuse them. Inspect the saved figure. Final answer only: saved filenames and a check table with equal-impedance maximum amplitude, zero-thickness maximum amplitude, baseline maximum amplitude at x=0, and baseline global maximum absolute amplitude with its distance and time. No interpretation yet: the handout explains the figure.
What you should see

A downloadable two-panel figure, executed numerical checks, and saved code and values. A code listing alone is not completion.

3
Minutes 15–25

Change the pulse, not the rocks

Do this

Before sending, predict aloud whether a shorter pulse might help distinguish the boundaries. “I am unsure” is fine. Send Prompt 2. Open wedge-frequency.png and wedge-traces.png.

Why: Only frequency changes. The three traces are calculated at the same 20 m thick bed, so changed appearance cannot be a new geological layer. The machine checks pulse duration; you compare shapes. The top-to-base time interval is the round trip through the sand. If GeoGPT adds a sentence calling that interval “one-way”, that label is incorrect; use the two-way definition here. No extra reply is needed.

End with “Finished. Return to the handout.” Do not append a question or an offer. First check figure captions and previous unit labels against the executed code. Correct misleading captions in the saved figures without changing the computed data. The interface times come from geometry and coincide only at zero thickness; they do not change with resolution. The top/base gap is two-way travel through the sand. A Ricker pulse has zero crossings at plus/minus 1/(pi*f*sqrt(2)); use the code-derived full width, not an inconsistent verbal formula. Do not equate the measured strongest amplitude thickness with an exact quarter wavelength. Briefly name any corrected label in one sentence. Then use our executed wedge, frequency figures and saved signed trace values to write a field-team note of no more than 100 words. Structure it as Question; Observation; Interpretation; Next evidence. Explain whether loss of two separately visible reflections proves the sand has ended, using a named location or frequency from the actual outputs. Separate the known hypothetical bed from a claim about real ground. State one useful independent borehole observation. Do not infer groundwater, hydrocarbons or permeability from amplitude. Use only a claim you can verify in those outputs. The wedge has zero thickness at x=0. Dashed interface times are supplied reference lines, not picked signal extrema; do not assert they always coincide. Include the saved figure filename a colleague should inspect. Finish the investigation without more questions.

Research context and source papers

Modern seismic studies use modelling to test alternative geological interpretations. This lesson teaches the controlled forward-model comparison underlying that work. Its simple two-reflection model is foundational, not a new imaging method or a real aquifer prediction.

The briefing above supplies what you need during class. These sources are for further study.
